newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Opposition strike shuts down business in Karachi.
newsitem.headline: Opposition strike shuts down business in Karachi.

text.p: A general strike called by the opposition ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) paralysed most trade and business activity in the Pakistani port city of Karachi on Saturday, witnesses said.
They said traffic was thin in the normally bustling city of 12 million people and most trade and commercial centres looked deserted.
"The volume of traffic is 50 to 70 percent less than is usual on working days, but private public transport is available in many parts of the city," a police official said.
Police and paramilitary rangers patrolled major roads and volatile MQM strongholds in central and eastern districts.
A police official said shops and other businesses had closed for fear of violence. Government offices and schools were closed for the weekend.

MQM spokesman Shoaib Bukhari said the strike had been called in protest against the "forced" induction of a MQM woman deputy, Feroza Begum, to the Sindh provincial cabinet by Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's ruling Pakistan People's Party.
Karachi is the capital of Sindh province.

"The government blackmailed Feroza Begum as her son, Usma Qadri, was under detention," he said. "They exploited the mother by threatening that her son could also be killed (if she did not join the government)."
The government has denied the MQM charge, saying Feroza had defected from her party and joined the government of her own free will.

The official APP news agency quoted Feroza as saying after taking the oath as a minister on Wednesday that she had joined the government to save youths, such as her son, who had gone into hiding and were unable to meet their parents.
Feroza is the second MQM member in the Sindh assembly to defect from the party. The MQM represents Urdu-speaking Mohajirs who originally migrated from India after the partition in 1947.
The government claims the MQM is responsible for most of the violence in Karachi which has claimed 350 lives this year. Last year's death toll reached more than 2,000.
The MQM blames the authorities for the bloodshed, citing what it terms extra-judicial killings of its activists while in custody.

The MQM has staged at least eight general strikes in Karachi this year, compared with 30 last year, mainly to protest against the deaths of members killed in what it describes as "fake encounters" with police.
